title: First days in New York and the union's restrictions
summary: Hodes arrives at Bill Kennedy's basement flat with a pregnant wife. He deposits his card at the union and hears all the can'ts and rules for out-of-town men.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, if you can imagine the -- a couple, just married, two dogs and the Ford full of all our possessions, our few records, just packed, you could barely see out of it. And we're in New York, and there we are. We're in this big town and we find our way way up North there, the Washington-something, where Bill Kennedy was living. And he's over there with open arms, come on in, a basement apartment, very little privacy, especially for a newly married couple. It's very embarrassing. Because she'd already gotten pregnant. So she couldn't wait to get out and get our own place. Within three months, she did.

But the next day I am on the subway, I'm taught how to go there, and I'm down on Elm, which is a main stem at night. I went to the union first and deposited my card, and they told me the whereabouts, what to do. Now, you can't do this and you can't do that and you can't do this. By the time they got through telling me all the can'ts, you feel like leaving town. Because --
You can't work out of town.

No, you can't work one night on a city gig, at that time. They wouldn't get you do that, either. Plus, I found out later on that most of the leaders were instructed not to encourage out of town men by giving them work. Their whole idea --
So you didn't have anything pending or anything.
